newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko stirs crowd with talk of WW2, Chernobyl.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko stirs crowd with talk of WW2, Chernobyl.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, facing a chorus of criticism from abroad, turned a crowd of about 10,000 people ecstatic on Tuesday by exploiting painful memories in Belarus of World War Two and the Chernobyl nuclear disaster.

While the United States, European officials, Russia and Ukraine expressed concern at a constitutional row which has pitted parliament and other institutions against him, the 42- year-old leader turned to the people for support.
"Dear people! There is a referendum on November 24. You will vote not for Lukashenko but for your lives, for the future of your children," he said.
Lukashenko is seeking approval for a new constitutional draft which would extend his term by more than two years to November 2001 and tighten his grip on all branches of power.

Most parliament deputies have joined forces to stop Lukashenko enforcing the results of the referendum, which he says will carry legal force despite a constitutional court ruling saying it should not.
Lukashenko sped into this small, charmless, military town of about 100,000 people 70 km (40 miles) east of Minsk in a big black Mercedes, heading an impressive motorcade of western-built vehicles.

Lukashenko, locked in a row with a parliament which is still known as the Supreme Soviet, addressed the crowd from the feet of a huge monument to Vladimir Lenin emblazoned with the words "All power to the Soviets!"

He invoked memories of World War Two, when Nazi forces overran the country between Russia and Poland. "Enough war! We have fought till we can fight no more. We buried every third person so that war would never come again," Lukashenko declared.
Most Belarussians can tell horror stories of relatives slaughtered in four years' occupation by Adolf Hitler's forces.
But after World War Two, the explosion at Chernobyl nuclear plant in 1986 is the disaster which most upsets Belarussians.

Referring to one of four questions proposed by him at the referendum on buying and selling land, Lukashenko said there could be no such privatisation because a quarter of the republic's territory was still contaminated.
More than 70 percent of the fallout from the reactor hit Belarus, affecting tens of thousands of people.
His opponents at home accuse him of building a dictatorship but Lukashenko says he is carrying out the people's will and has begun a tour of towns which has drawn huge crowds.

"You should not fear, there is no dictatorship, there is no fascism, and fascism will never return to our land," he told the crowd, which interrupted his 30-minute speech several times with rapturous applause and cries of "Hurrah! Hurrah!"
"We will live together. We will build this life together. I promise you that I will always be with you. Only you have the right to criticise, strike or beat up the president," he said.
The crowd, mostly elderly, were overwhelmed by the appearance of their lean, angular, moustachioed president who they call "batska" in Belarussian -- or father.

Nikolai Burdyka, a pensioner in a greasy brown raincoat explained why he would support Lukashenko. "He's a great man. He speaks for the people. He lives for the people. We really like him because he speaks so simply and so clearly."
They waved the state's red and green flag and former Soviet flags as veterans of the Soviet Union's bloody and prolonged war in Afghanistan gave a warm-up concert of military songs.

One veteran, apparently referring to officials who have been sacked or resigned, including the prime minister who resigned on Monday: "The rats are abandoning ship, but it is not sinking. The ship is sailing surely on to a bright future."
The concept of a "bright future" was the cornerstone of ideology in the Soviet era, for which Lukashenko -- and many impoverished Belarussians -- often expresses nostalgia.
